p: Yes, we place them by their homes. We also make sure that, you know, the assistant school safety agents, it fills in the elementary schools. So that leaves a passageway for them to turn into school safety agents. So, to become an assistant school safety agent, you have to be 18 years of age. So, by the time they hit 21 years of age, they can too be– it’s a pathway into becoming a school safety agent.
Thank you.

That’s how we attempt to retain them as well. And we lose a good bit of our school safety agents to becoming police officers as well. And we do voluntary overtime if, you know, we need to. It’s a need-to basis. That’s how we help to retain them financially as well.

Alright. Same questions for 911 operators. How's the headcount? What’s the budgeted headcount? What’s the actual headcount? How’s retention? Last preliminary hearing advocates testified that there was a shortage.
Yep.
Due to burnout.

We made significant progress, as I’ve mentioned in 911. I’m just looking for the actual numbers. Here we go. Our budgeted headcount for police communications technicians is 1,412 and we are shy of that by about 125, although we plan to put in a new class soon, I think in a month or two. So, we plan to hire about 100 new PCT’s in June, which will get us right up to that budgeted headcount which is fantastic.
What’s the starting salary for 911 operators? Is retention an issue?

Starting salary is $45,703 and it rises to $47,222 after one year. Top pay is $61,883, which you can achieve after three years. We have been in conversations with the Office of Labor Relations to try to increase the salary during the next contract negotiation.

Alright. Same questions for school crossing guards. That’s one issue that I’m consistently hearing about any time I visit a Community Board, members of the community are saying that they’ve been requesting for years a school crossing guard due to traffic safety issues around

their elementary schools. So, just wondering about staffing, what’s the actual headcount? How’s retention, and what are issues that we’re having with hiring? And before you answer, I just want to recognize the Riverdale Country Day School who has joined us. Thank you and welcome to the– to City Hall.

Alright, we’re doing well with school crossing guards. As of March 1st, we employed 2,123 school crossing guard level one’s, which is less than 100 below our budgeted headcount of 2,219. And for the level two’s, we’re at 78, which is 12 below the budgeted headcount of 90. We’re doing very nicely with school crossing guards.

Okay. Moving onto the questions related to the Bronx and also the new Bronx Patrol Borough South. So, you mentioned there’s going to be approximately 200 new police officers in the Bronx due to the division of the patrol borough. These are going to be new hires, correct, and if yes, why new hires? Why not experienced police officers?

No, we will do transfers into the boroughs. So, no, the 200 officers will be

transferred in. They won’t be straight out of the academy.

Okay. And talk to us about crime in the Bronx. So you mentioned that, you know, not that crime is down in the Bronx, but you mentioned some numbers which would signal progress, but you know, the CompStat report shows that murder is up by 26 percent this year compared to last year. Rape is up by 12.4 percent, shooting victims 35.7 percent, shooting incidents 29.7 percent. And of course, as I mentioned in my opening statement, public safety is a shared responsibility. Police officers cannot do it alone. But just curious, what is the plan to help resolve this crisis, this emergency that the Bronx is clearly in?

Okay. So, as of today, major crime in the borough of the Bronx this year is down 10.3 percent. It is– that borough is leading the city in terms of the overall crime reductions. I just want to make sure that we do not lose sight of that. The other point that I want to make is beyond what is on paper, we– well, let me just go through. The 10 percent reduction in the seven major crimes in the Bronx is felony assaults down 3.2 percent,

robberies down 10.6 percent, burglary down 19.2 percent, grand larceny down 12.4 percent, and auto theft down 16.8 percent. Last year, in the borough of the Bronx and citywide we saw double-digit declines both in murders and in shootings. We saw an 18 percent drop in murder and a 25 decline in shootings in that borough.
That was last year?
The way we– that was last year. We’re three months from last year.
Right.

The way we achieved those record numbers was using our violence reduction plan, where we– or one of the things we did, which is taking hundreds of new officers out of the academy, putting them on foot posts on the streets and in the locations and at the times where they are needed most specifically to address gun violence. That plan worked incredibly well this year. I also want to be clear that the Bronx as a borough got the vast majority of the new recruits, the foot posts, the people that we assigned to work foot posts. It got way more than any other borough in the City of New York.

So, the resources are there. The staffing in Bronx Patrol Commands is up. We are doing this additional split that is going to add more focus, attention, specialty units and officers to the borough, and Chief LiPetri can add now more about what his crime fighting strategies have been to address this slight uptick that you are seeing over the past two months.

So, just, you know, the Commissioner spoke about the reduction in shootings and– the Bronx led the city in reduction of shooting incidents last year, led the city of New York with over 100 less shooting victims. We have seen a slight uptick in violence in the Bronx. We attribute it to three factors, some narcotics-related shootings, some Krewe-related shootings, and we do have a small uptick in some of our licensed and unlicensed premises. We’ve identified 17 violence reduction zones in the Bronx, the most in any patrol borough. We’ve been deploying to those zones since the beginning of the year, and while we’re deployed to those zones, we’ve had one shooting in those 17 violence reduction zones. We talk about precision policing, not just

with field deployment, though field deployment is the number one crime strategy for the New York City Police Department, it’s also about precision investigations into krewes that plague the Bronx community, and I want to give an example. There is a specific krewe that lives and– really lives within two housing developments, in Melrose Jackson. They were an organized younger krewe, and our gun violence suppression division looked at that. We analyzed that with our criminal group database, and we saw that they were most, if not the most violent krewe, one of the top three most violent krewes in New York City, and once we arrested them and prosecuted them, we have a 40 percent reduction in shootings in the 40 precinct directly attributed to phenomenal gang/krewe takedown using precision policing, data, and some great investigative work. But again, it starts with field deployment. By far the Bronx gets the most field deployment and also precision. You want to look at three commands in the Bronx right now, the 41 precinct down 25 percent in crime, the 43 down 22 percent in crime, the 44 down 18 percent in crime. The 46 Morris Heights section of the Bronx last year saw a 54 percent reduction in

shooting incidents. It is– we are laser-focused to continue to drive down crime, not just in the Bronx.

So, I would just end by saying I find it to be an unfair characterization of the current state to say that major crime in the Bronx is up. In fact, it is down and it is down big, and it is down bigger than any borough. It is also the case that on last year’s record-breaking shooting numbers that included over 100 fewer shootings in the borough of the Bronx last– what’s that? I’m sorry, 100 shooting victims in the Borough of the Bronx last year, are we up slightly on it, yes, but we are working the same play book doing the same things, and on top of that creating a new patrol borough, and I have every confidence that we are being– acting responsibly.

Right. And you know, the numbers support some of your points, right? Robbery is down 10 percent and etcetera, and if you take all the crime categories, maybe those numbers show a specific point, but I’m specifically referring to the progress that the city has made on the issue of gun

violence. Shootings are down citywide in the Bronx. They’re up 35.7 percent.
Yes, we understand that, and I spoke to it.
So it’s safe to say that the progress related to shootings hasn’t reached the Bronx–
[interposing] Last year, there were over–
[interposing] At least on that specific issue.
100 fewer people shot in the Borough of the Bronx than the previous year. Last year–
[interposing] Talking about this year.
The single largest shooting declines were in the Borough of the Bronx. So, the year just ended.
[interposing] I’m talking about this year, though.

We have had three months of this year, let’s look at the data, but I am telling you we are using the same playbook that we used last

year, which led to record-breaking results citywide, but particularly in the Borough of the Bronx.
Okay. So, I’ll conclude that topic on the Bronx crime, but you know, we made progress last year but it seems like we’re going backwards.

This year is probably the second safest year for shooting incidents and shooting victims in the Borough of the Bronx ever. I will confirm that, but I don’t want you to– I don’t want this to be mischaracterized. We are seeing really huge amount of progress on crime fighting generally, particularly gun violence generally citywide.
You know, the Police Commissioner said it, but I just want to– the Bronx right now leads the City of New York in overall crime reduction. Leads the City of New York.
Right, but I’m talking about shootings and murders, though.

We understand the small up– we understand the small uptick in gun violence, and there’s– you know, New York City Police Department is

front and center to reduce violence, not just in the Bronx, but in the city.

Okay, cool. So, I’ll move onto the next point, but again, I get it. We made progress in general when you consider all the crime categories, but the numbers related to shooting victims and shooting incidents and murder are going up this year compared to last year. That is–
[interposing] Yes, compared to last year it is up slightly–
[interposing] Those are numbers that we cannot ignore under any circumstance.
And last year was a record-breaking year for gun violence, and I will not have the work of the members of the New York City Police Department mischaracterized.

Okay. Moving on to vehicle theft. So throughout the city we’ve seen a drastic increase in vehicle wheel– not even vehicles, specifically their wheels. There’s a few pages that I follow on social media run by members of my community. I know the precinct that I’m in that’s a big target. Every single day there’s new pictures of cars basically on the floor, no wheels, and based on

the pictures and the videos that I've seen it seems like it’s the same krewe basically literally working 24/7. I’m making that assumption because there’s been a few videos of the same exact white BMW basically removing the wheels within seconds, and it seems like this has been going on for years, and I speak to members of my community, they feel basically helpless given that every single day it’s five or 10 new cars. So, just wondering– I’m sure all of you know about this issue. What’s being done about this? Has there been any investigations, any arrests?

Of course there have been investigations. This year, thefts of tires and rims are down 30 percent citywide. Auto crime works on a number of long-term cases. I’ll be very honest. There are not meaningful consequences for this type of crime in the City of New York unless we are able to put together long-term cases, which is what we are doing, but onesie, twosie [sp?], there are no consequences in our criminal justice system for stealing tires and rims in practice. And so the Police Department can– no pun intended- keep spinning our wheels, but that is one

thing that you should look at if you have concerns about thefts of tires and rims.

I just want to add, the Bronx this year in tire and rim theft is down 45 percent, 45 percent. So, it leads, again, the city as far as percentage reduction and I know the Police Commissioner alluded to it that tire and rim thefts are down 31 percent citywide led by the Bronx. Yes, we do have internal investigations into these krewes, obviously very sensitive, and we are deployed specifically– mainly on the midnight tours to focus on these types of thefts along with other vehicular accessory thefts like airbags and sensors. And I talked about it just before a phenomenal arrest last night in the Bronx. Though the krewe went over to the Queens. We’re very focused on intelligence aspect of that. We operationalized that intelligence, and we ended up arresting two individuals.
Arrested how many you said?
Two.

Got it. A few questions, these are from– speaking with our wonderful Bronx

Borough President last night, by the way, former Chair of the Public Safety Committee. She had a few questions that she wanted me to ask. Any updates on the Rodman’s Neck Firing Range renovation project in the Bronx? And also number two, has the NYPD thought about creating a Harbor Unit for the Bronx?
We thought about what?
Creating a Harbor Unit for the Bronx.
No, we have not thought about creating a Harbor Unit for the Bronx. And Kristine, could you please answer the question in Rodman’s Neck?

Yes, on Rodman’s Neck, we’re commencing the work there. There’s a lot of infrastructure work that needs to be done. So, it’ll– you’re not going to see new building structures for a while, but essentially we’ve started and the phases one, two, and three which are creating a facility storage building, working on the underground utilities like I said, and then the utility work throughout the facility, new sewage, new electric, everything that’s needed there to do the state of the art training facility. The project is

on schedule and it’s expected to be completed in the summer of 2029.

What are factors that you would consider when thinking about creating a Harbor Unit? My understanding is– not my district, but my understanding is that the city island section of the Bronx has issues in their waters and generally they rely on the police from Queens or the Harbor Unit from Queens to help resolve issues in the Bronx. So, what are factors that would–

[interposing] Given that we’re not considering it at this time, I want to provide you a follow-up answer where we can be more thoughtful about what factors we would consider, but it’s not under consideration at this time.
Okay. So, I’ll pass it on to Council Member Encarnacion for a second round of questions, and then Council Member Wong.

I actually– so I know the last round of questions I just threw in a narcotics question. So I wanted to kind of give it some context. I know that many of the issues that we’re seeing in the Bronx, also in East Harlem. I serve both Manhattan and the Bronx– around the 125th

Street is really around drug selling. It’s the drugs that are being sold there. You know, the car jackings, the thefts, the retail thefts, a lot of it is about buying drugs. And so I wanted to kind of get an idea of what the stats are in terms of– you know, I haven’t heard of like big drug busts, things like that that are happening in those communities specifically but also just around communities that have high levels of shootings or theft. I mean, the retail theft–
[interposing] You want to know our narcotics enforcement numbers?
Correct.
We can get you– I mean, we probably don’t have it here for your specific precincts, but we can get you– follow up with our narcotics enforcement numbers across your commands.
Yeah. And really, it is also a plug, because I know that as we look how do we–
[interposing] Oh, the Chief has it.

I don’t have like specifics, but I could just tell you this. Last year in the City of

New York there was over a 20 percent increase in narcotics arrests, with the Bronx leading the number one borough with over 7,500 narcotics arrests. I’ve had personal conversations with DA Clarke, and you know, her top leadership and specifically have given them 13 blocks or areas within the Bronx that really are plagued by narcotics deals and use, and we have really seen, you know, a nice partnership with some of the consequences that we need to see when it comes to arresting these individuals.
Thank you for that. And then in the 17 violence reduction zones, how do you see those being broken up once we break up north and south Bronx? Like where do most of the– where will most of them–

So, I would say the south would probably get more than the north just because, again, the data mining and data analytics that goes through it, also with a little bit of a historical knowledge on it. But I would say the south would have more than enough.

I also have to say that the characterization that underserved communities are not experiencing the same crime reductions that the rest

of the city are experiencing in the opening statement, that’s entirely wrong. The communities that have been historically plagued by gun violence are leading the crime reductions in the City of New York, because that is where we are putting our field training officers and our resources on foot posts to prevent the gun violence.
And I understand that. Leading in crime reduction doesn’t mean that there isn’t crime anymore there, right? They were very–
[interposing] Of course not.
High numbers to begin with.

And the work certainly continues, but what I am reacting to was the Chair’s characterization of the fact that parts of the city with gun vi– or with historically high levels of gun violence are not experiencing the same reductions over the past year and a half or year in three months. They certainly are leading the way.

Commissioner, respectfully, I was just reciting the information on the CompStat

which shows that shooting victims, 35.7 percent increase, shooting incidents 29.7, so–
[interposing] Yes, over our record–
[interposing] I was saying–
[interposing] Over a record low year, and I agree with you that–
[interposing] I was just reciting information that’s public information.

I like to set records every year and I intend to do that this year, including in the Borough of the Bronx, but I do not appreciate the mischaracterization of the general work of the Department. What you said in your opening statement that the underserved communities in this city are not experiencing the same reductions that other parts of the city are. In fact, they are leading them, and they are leading them because that is where I have put this department’s resources.

Oh no, I was just waiting to see– you’re good? Okay. I think– because I think my question was around crossing guards. We took care of that. And then the khaki pants unit

which we also addressed as well. That’s my word for them. I know it’s not the official name. I think all of the questions that I had for the second round were answered. Thank you so much.
Thank you. Now, Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair. Commissioner, in my district it’s been years and years that there’s huge problems on abandoned cars, cars with fake plates, fake insurance stickers. People move here from out of state and decide to leave their cars there, because it’s an industrial area, and then they leave them weeks or even months, and I want to thank the Transportation Bureau and the traffic agents who work in and around my district. They have been extremely responsive, and they do everything they can with the resources they have. My question is there any plans in this fiscal plan to increase the headcount for traffic enforcement agents citywide and especially in Queens North?

So, on traffic enforcement agents we are not yet to our budgeted headcount, and so no, we are not now requesting additional traffic enforcement agents. But I agree with you, I am very

proud of the work that has been done on row tows. If you look at– which is really addressing abandoned and derelict vehicles. 2024, we had 25,760, 2025 was over 34,000 removals.

Okay. Please see if there’s a possibility if you can increase the headcount. The other limitations is that we hear is pound space. There’s only so much room to store vehicles, especially chronic illegal parkers and abandoned cars. Are there any plans to expand pound capacity?
Yes, our Deputy Commissioner of Management and Budget, Kristine Ryan, can answer that.

So, we are still unfortunately working with reduced space after the closure of the Manhattan poundage. You can imagine real estate is very expensive in the City of Manhattan, so it has been a challenge to find a piece of real estate that fits, that will work, and that also be done with limited fiscal resources. So we have been, you know, towing as we can to the Bronx tow pound in the north. We take the north half of Manhattan and the other in south, but Queens

citywide, we do rely also on an outside vendor to help with some of our vehicles as well. So, we’re trying to make this work, but–

[interposing] Closing the Manhattan tow pound really put enormous strain on the entire system, and I don’t think that was a well-conceived or well thought out decision. We should be careful before we close police facilities willy-nilly.

Okay, thank you. My next questions regarding auxiliary officers. They volunteer their time often late at night, and we knew from past tragedies that their work can put them in real danger. My understanding is that many auxiliaries are now operating with expired bullet-resistant vests. What is the current condition and replacement schedule for auxiliary vests, and has the Department requested funding in this financial plan to fully replace them.
We certainly have.
Yes, we have requested funding to replace the vests for the auxiliary officers.
Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. No more questions.

Thank you so much, Council Member Wong. I have some few final questions, and then we’ll conclude. We have a very lengthy agenda. We’ll hear from our District Attorneys next. I know we’re a little bit behind schedule. So, a few questions. On the– I guess I’ll start with the bomb squad. Recently, as we saw at Gracie Mansion and the surrounding area, there was a bomb threat. What is the budgeted and actual headcount for the NYPD bomb squad, and do you have sufficient equipment for the bomb squad like the disposal robots?
The headcount for the bomb squad is 37, totalling approximately $6 million in PS costs. What’s the other part of the question?
Do you have sufficient equipment for the bomb squad like the–
You know, it’s funny. I’m actually with– just spoke to the CO of the bomb squad and meeting with him soon to go over any new requests that they have for equipment.

At the Executive Budget hearing I heard you talk about some of the non-lethal equipment at our officer’s disposal like tasers and the OC spray, mace. What other equipment does an officer have access to? I saw a video with officers with shields.
So, patrol officers are equipped with tasers, with expandable batons, with straight batons, with OC pepper spray, and they have access to protective shields.
Last year I heard the contract for tasers was $11 million. I wanted to get an update on the cost of that contract and also the new transition to the Taser 7 or go beyond the newest model?

So, the current cost for the Taser 7 is $10.7 million. That includes 10,000 devices and cartridges for all members of service. That’s both training and field usage. The NYPD is currently piloting the Taser 10 with the most recent rollout for the Emergency Services Unit.

Alright. Thank you for the information. Anyone else has any other questions? Alright, so I think we are concluded with the first

part of this hearing. Thank you so much for joining today. Thank you for the testimony, and thank you for all the work you do. [break]

Good afternoon, ladies and gentleman. If you’re here for the Public Safety Preliminary hearing, you’re in the right place. Keep it down please. Let’s keep it down. If you’re here for the Public Safety Preliminary hearing, you’re in the right place. Before we start, make sure you silence all electronic devices, and please do not approach the dais at any time. If you need assistance, just get the attention of one of the Sergeant at Arms, and we’d be more than happy to assist you with whatever– with whoever you need to meet. In the meantime, make yourself comfortable, please. We should be starting shortly.

Please settle down. Please settle down. We’re going to begin shortly. Please find your seats. Settle down, guys. Please find your seats. Thank you. And also, update, no one approaching the dais. Please, no one is to approach the dais.

[gavel]

Welcome, District Attorneys and also Special Narcotics Prosecutor, to our Public Safety budget hearing. It’s great to see you all again. Thank you for being here, and also thank you for all the work you do. I’ll provide time for all of you to make an opening statement and then we’ll ask questions, but before that I’m going to pass it briefly to the Committee Counsel to swear all of you in, and then we’ll start with your opening statements starting with the Bronx District Attorney, and we’ll go from right to left. And we are joined today by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez, Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz, Staten Island District Attorney Michael McMahon, and Special Narcotics Prosecutor Bridget Brennan.

If you could all please raise your right hands? Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this Committee and respond honestly to Council Member

questions? Noting that all witnesses answered affirmatively, you may begin your testimony.

Is this on? Good morning. Oh, good afternoon. Good afternoon, Public Safety Chair, Oswald Feliz– I don’t see Finance Chair Linda Lee– and all the members of the Public Safety Committee, Council Member Encarnacion, Phil Wong, Sandy Nurse, Kamillah Hanks, thank you all for being here this morning. Thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak with you today. I am Darcel Clark, Bronx District Attorney. I’ve just spent 10 years of delivering justice. This year marks my 10th anniversary as Bronx District Attorney. There are many challenges to serve the 1.4 million people of the Bronx, but undoubtedly, these have been the most rewarding years of my life. I owe a tremendous debt of gratitude to the ADAs and professional staff who stood beside me over the years and modeling excellence. To each staff member, present and former, I say thank you. The Bronx is safer and better because of you. You inspire me as we pursue justice with integrity together. Recently, a Daily News front page headline described the Bronx as the most deadly

borough. The article provided data showing that the Bronx has suffered half of the city’s murders thus far this year. My prosecutors and NYPD worked swiftly to charge defendants in 10 of those cases already. But to me, they’re not just cases or stats. Every death represents a person who belonged to a family, a community in the Bronx. Each person has people who love them and mourn them, from a father and hardworking Uber driver shot by a man who crashed into his car, to a 16-year-old high school football player who was forced to run from shots fired near a McDonald’s, to an unsuspecting 19-year-old man shot randomly while walking down the street at two o’clock in the afternoon. Behind each violent incident there’s an underlying truth, the borough in direst need of help receives the least resources. My testimony today echoes my pleas before the City Council two years ago. The neighborhoods suffering from high rates of poverty and crime remain the same as when I was a child. The tragic difference today is that more of our youth have access to guns, creating a spike in youth

violence. The Bronx has 20 percent of the city’s youth population, 30 percent of youth gun arrests, and nearly half of the youth arrested for shootings. Here’s the sad fact, more than a third of the city’s youth shooting victims are in the Bronx. Too many kids are losing their future to the barrel of a gun. My borough needs resources that will encourage our young people to seize an opportunity over picking up a gun. Opportunities improve chances to improve employment, access to education, pathways to housing, and open doors to mental health and substance abuse services, addressing the underlying conditions that lead to crime. These resources are not optional. They are necessities, tangible investments that will bolster our community and provide hope. They are concrete solutions for reducing crime and improving our community. And when the Bronx succeeds, the city succeeds. My office is doing our part. We held several reentry and employment fairs throughout the year with a focus on neighborhoods where many formerly incarcerated people reside. Each event leaves me more inspired. At one fair, I was approached by a

man who was recently paroled. He was there getting an ID, trying on a donated suit to wear to a job interview, and speaking with potential employers. He said to me, I can’t believe that you’re doing this, and he kept saying that to me, and he said thank you. This is a small example of how my office intentionally serves the people of the Bronx who need more. Given the community needs, our budget requests focus on therapy for crime victims, revitalizing youth justice, holistic engagement for families in violent neighborhoods, alternatives to prosecution and incarceration and detention, and continued support for South Bronx Community Justice Center. The NYPD submitted 52,211 arrests in the Bronx to the Bronx District Attorney’s office in 2025, a nine percent increase from 2024, and a 22 percent increase since 2019. In 2025, our Crime Victims Assistance Bureau delivered free support service to 8,774 new and existing clients, 493 of them were children. CVAB provided nearly 55,000 direct assistance services and referrals to victims of sexual assault, domestic violence, human trafficking, and elder abuse.

Our trauma therapist provided 22,000 sessions to 230 new clients and 74 pre-existing clients. They provided trauma therapy to 60 children. We provide all of these services without costs, regardless of whether there is an active criminal case. I stand with victims of crimes and their families. I stood with the parents of Nicholas Domenici [sp?], the toddler killed by exposure to fentanyl in a home daycare center that was a front for a narcotics operation, fulfilling my promise that the operators of the daycare would face justice in the Bronx for their beautiful son’s murder, and on March 4th I stood with them as the defendants were sentenced to 25 years to life. CVAB advocates and therapists were there, too, and will be with them for as long as they need them. Unfortunately, CVAB has a shortage of therapists. To bridge this gap in service, we’re asking for $2.2 million dollars in fiscal year 2027 and $2.1 million in baseline funding to hire more therapists. When considering our youth, I note that we raise the age, but now we must lift a generation by revitalizing the youth justice system to stem the

loss of our young people to gun violence, death, and prison. I established a Youth Justice Bureau with ADAs and professional staff, all of whom have been trained on adolescent development, programming, alternative dispositions that are available to hold youth accountable when appropriate. During its first year, the Youth Justice Bureau screened all juvenile and adolescent matters through a youth justice lens and strengthened relationships with the courts, law enforcement, community partners and service providers. When staffing is complete, the Bureau’s prosecutors will handle all cases involving youth defendants. This bureau is piloting an initiative called the Justice Innovation for Bronx Youth, or JIBY, as we call it. The goal of this program is to serve high-risk youth with partners providing critical screenings, case management services, and an assessment tool and training, mental health and substance use services, credible messengers, and spiritual guidance. The JIBY pilot is funded in part by a federal grant of $650,000 over three years. To receive these

funds, our office must max the funding received over three years. I’m asking the city to provide $600,000 to cover the total cost of this pilot. Upon its success, it will serve as a template for expansion. In January, I held a youth justice stakeholder’s convening to increase cross-agency and cross-sector partnerships and identify practical strategies for prevention, intervention, diversion, and re-entry support. Our shared goal is to build a more equitable, effective youth justice system in New York City. There was a consensus among the 40+ participants that the city should seek further resources. I am informed– I informed the stakeholders that since Raise the Age Law was passed and funded as part of the state budget in 2017, the city has been excluded from receiving state funds. I’m pleased to report that the Assembly will include a new proposal to make New York City eligible to receive state funding to support expenses for Raise the Age, and the Senate has a bill to carve out $50 million to establish the Youth Justice Innovation Fund. Another resource my office developed is called Bronx Restore, a prevention and engagement program

for 30 high-risk individuals in the St. Marys Park area and Fordham area which have high rates of gun violence and other violent offenses. The state invested $3 million in this public health approach to the root causes of violence. Community-based partners provide a stipend for participants who partake in trauma therapy, job readiness, financial literacy, conflict resolution, restorative justice, internship opportunities, mentorship and case management. For years I have been advocating for a South Bronx Community Justice Center. The Mayor’s Office and the City Council each allocated $1 million in operating costs for the city-owned site at 630 Jackson Avenue at the nexus of Motthaven, Melrose, and Morrisania, and I have to tell you, I’m deeply appreciative of that. However, there are significant additional costs in capital expenses. I ask that the city make the South Bronx Community Justice Center a priority now by committing to baseline operational costs and funding capital expenses for renovations, upgrades and repairs of the site.

Every other borough has at least one justice center. The Bronx is long overdue to have its own. In closing, I’m here today proud of my exceptional staff and advocating for the 1.4 million people of the Bronx. Their admirable persistence, resilience, fortitude and optimism, in a word, their grit, represents the best of this great city. When the Bronx succeeds, again, the city succeeds. The Bronx is not only where I serve, it’s the place that I’ve always called home. For me, this is personal. I speak from my heart, and I hope that you will take it to heart. Thank you very much for your time.

Good afternoon. Certainly a hard act to follow. It’s been my privilege and honor to serve those 10 years alongside DA Clark as District Attorney of Staten Island. Good afternoon. My name is Michael McMahon, and I’m also honored to sit here with my other colleagues who represent the best in prosecution, not only in our city, but in our country. Some of us are also alumni of this august body and it’s always a pleasure to come, if you will, and I thank you, Chairman Feliz and

Minority Whip– Majority Whip Kamillah Hanks from the great borough of Staten Island, Council Member Encarnacion, Council Member Nurse, and Council Member Wong. Thank you for your attention to our testimony today and giving us the opportunity to discuss with you these very important issues. As Staten Island’s chief law enforcement officer, I am incredibly proud of all the work we have done in my office. Together with our partners in the NYPD, neighboring law enforcement agencies, and all of our partners who call our beloved Staten Island home to make our borough a safer place. While there remains much work to be done, everybody here today should be encouraged by the record-low crime numbers reported on Staten Island last year. Violent crime, particularly homicides and shootings, reached historic lows in our borough in 2025. For the third straight year, Staten Island recorded double-digit decreases in stolen vehicles. Catalytic converter thefts were down over 90 percent in 2025, and as I stand here or sit here before you today, incidents of retail theft are down almost 50 percent on Staten Island.

Additionally, we also saw encouraging progress in our fight against the opioid and overdose epidemic with Staten Island recording a 49 percent decrease in opioid overdose deaths, the largest decrease in all of New York City. And while Staten Island proudly remains the safest community of 500,000 residents in the country, now is not the time for us or anyone else to take a victory lap. We know that domestic violence, youth crime, and the omnipresence of scams remain massive public safety issues for Staten Islanders and their families, and we are committed with your help to doing everything in our power to turn the tide and help restore both public safety and peace of mind back to our beloved borough. However, in order to do that, we need the administration and this Council’s help. During my testimony before you last year and the year before that, I warned the Council that Staten Island was facing a dire shortage of uniformed police officers and detectives in our borough. Despite our persistent pleas, Staten Island has 20 percent fewer cops patrolling our shores now than we did five years ago, and fewer cops deployed on

Staten Island than there were in 1968 when our population was half the size it is today. Our borough, and New York City as a whole, needs the uniformed personnel and staffing necessary to prevent, deter, and properly investigate crime. Now is not the time to roll back the gains that have been made. A persistent but underrated significant driver of crime on Staten Island and one where we as a city must dedicate more resources to combatting is domestic violence. A terrible reality that impacts far too many families and we know goes widely under-reported. On Staten Island domestic violence helped to drive a significant increase, more than 25 percent, in incidents of rape last year, as well as a majority of felony assaults committed in our borough. As it stands now, domestic violence accounts for nearly a quarter of all index crimes committed on Staten Island. And while we thank this body for supporting the creation of our Intimate Partner Sexual Violence Unit, we once again ask that our City Council Members support the life-saving work of our domestic violence bureau and victim services unit and continue the DOVE funding allocations.

While there are many pressing public issues– safety challenges, none are more important right now as the alarming increase in youth crime and the harmful impact of New York State’s Raise the Age Laws. Raise the Age reforms began with the laudable goal of minimizing the exposure of 16 and 17 year olds to the adult criminal justice system. Half a decade later, however, our communities have seen the flaws in this approach that was adopted. All too frequently, adolescent offenders face little to no consequences for serious crimes, including a majority of gun crimes and the most violent assaults. Furthermore, courts and prosecutors are forced to disregard patterns of violence and recidivism and victims lose access to justice when cases are re-routed to the Family Court system. Unfortunately, the numbers support this growing concern. Overall, youth arrests were up 44 percent on Staten Island last year with felony youth arrests increasing by nearly 54 percent. Even more concerning, as of this month, 12 percent of New York City’s shooting victims are between the ages of 10

and 17; 21 percent of shooting perpetrators fall within that same group, age group. Over a quarter of all gun arrests on Staten Island last year involved individuals under the age of 20. Numbers on paper can feel abstract, but in the real world, numbers are not statistics, they are lives. Arrests are up, victims are up. How can anyone say that the law is working as intended and doesn’t need to be tweaked. It is for these reasons and more that my office remains dedicated to addressing the underlying conditions of crime while encouraging supportive programming that builds families and our youth up. Thanks to vital funding allocated by this body, RCDA has partnered with the Center for Justice Innovation to actively engage and support at-risk youth impacted by the criminal justice system. With $635,000 coming from RCDA and an additional $125,000 coming from the City Council discretionary funding, CJI maintains a wide variety of youth programming, including restorative and peer facilitated diversion programming, leadership development, violence prevention and community healing, place making, and so much more.

Once a young person ends up in Family Court or before us in the youth part of Criminal Court, they have likely experienced so much trauma and missed countless opportunities for intervention. That is why programming like that being offered by CJI and their partner organizations is so critically important because an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of prosecution, particularly in the case of our kids. I am equally proud to share that my office utilizes close to 40 different diversion programs from a variety of different providers, ensuring that nearly 40 percent of all arrestees on Staten Island are offered some sort of an alternative to incarceration. However, for far too long, Richmond County District Attorney’s Office has done this critical work with one arm tied behind our backs. Staten Island remains without a Community Justice Center, and while we graciously received $5 million in capital money two years ago at the request of Council Member Hanks, capital funding is desperately needed to correct this inequity and bring this dream to fruition.

As my office continues to work tirelessly to combat these challenges, our success depends entirely on us working together to make our city as safe as possible. We have remained vigilant and consistent in our dedication to the rule of law, to the protection of victims of crime, as well as the rights of the accused and the overall improvement of public safety on Staten Island. But I must reiterate in the strongest possible terms, as always, we need your help. With that said, I will focus the remainder of my testimony on highlighting our greatest challenges as well as our priority budget needs for Fiscal 2027 with fuller explanation of them in the written testimony that we submitted. First and foremost, as I mentioned, Staten Island is the only borough without a physical Community Justice Center. We have an old courthouse identified as a site. It needs a capital ingestion of– infusion of money, and with that we could give Staten Islanders the same advantages to getting out of the criminal justice system that others have in the rest of the city, and we request your help for that.

Second, we would request the addition of three felony Assistant District Attorneys to the Domestic Violence Bureau. Right now– we created for the first time a free-standing domestic violence bureau in Staten Island. We continue to focus on that issue. It is a major one for us, and we need the personnel and the people trained to deal with victimcentric prosecutions, and with your help we could make that a reality. We would like your help in expanding the workload of our Juvenile Justice Unit by giving us the funding to hire the personnel necessary to deal with the youth crimes that both myself and DA Clark have already outlined and what a challenge they are for us. Fourth, the issue of cyber security and scams is real. I’m sure your constituents are telling you about all the phishing email and texts that they get and how they are victims of that, and we would like to train and have each one of our felony bureaus someone who is trained in the area of cyber crimes. So whether it’s around a domestic violence crime or a traditional grand larceny, that we would be able to investigate and prosecute those cases.

As we all know, mental health is a major crisis in the City of New York and our country, and so we have a request for hiring experts in the mental health substance use disorder and alternative to incarceration unit so that we can better provide people who are in mental health distress and to try to keep them out of jail or prison. And then lastly, I believe we’re the only– we like to say that on Staten Island. We’re the only ones who don’t have a General Counsel in the office, and as our office has grown in size and importance in the issues that it deals with, we would like your help to have the funding to hire a general counsel so that the men and women in our office and issues of employment have the same rights and protections that other city employees have, and that we can provide– continue to work to strive to be the type of office that the people of Staten Island deserve. I want to thank you for your time, attention, and consideration of my testimony. It would be my pleasure at the end to answer any questions, and we look forward to our continued partnership with the New York City Council, in particular Council Member Hanks and Carr and Morano, our representatives,

striving to make Staten Island the best place that it can be and the safest and strongest community that it possibly can be. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Oswald Feliz, to all the members of the committee, and of course, to Council Member Sandy Nurse, as I am her constituent. It’s good to see all of you here today. It’s an honor to join my colleagues, and I appreciate the opportunity to share in the progress we’ve made in Brooklyn improving safety and fairness, and I ask the City Council for your continued support. I’m happy to report that last year was a record year in Brooklyn. In 2025, Brooklyn set a new standard in safety with the lowest number of homicides and the lowest number of shootings since the NYPD began keeping these statistics. That momentum has continued so far this year. Homicides are down an additional 64 percent from last year’s historic lows, and shootings are down approximately 15 percent. As someone who grew up in one of the toughest neighborhoods in New York City in East New York in the 80s and 90s, this transformation is truly incredible. I’m grateful for the hard work of my

staff and our partners in the NYPD, and of course, the many community leaders and partners who show up every day in the county to do the hard work. But while we’re setting new standards for safety, the Brooklyn DAs office remains hampered by a structural funding inequity rooted in the cost of our rented commercial office space. We remain the only District Attorney’s office without space in any municipal buildings. Brooklyn prosecutes the highest case volume in the city by far. Last year it was approximately 80,000 cases, 79,000 and change. We’re up five percent this year. Looking like we’ll be over 80,000 this year. We also serve the largest population, one of the most diverse populations, and we handle thousands more felonies than any other borough, including thousands of more violent felony offenses. But because Brooklyn has such a large part of our budget consumed by rent, what’s left over to actually do our work is severely compressed. When you adjust for the cost of our office space, our peer office is some, have up to 51 percent more funding per arrest than Brooklyn. I’ll say that again, 51 percent more per arrest than Brooklyn. The

disparities are also– if you look at by resident, they’re even more stark. Two of the offices have 80 percent more funding than Brooklyn per resident served after accounting for rent. Now, my point is not that any of my colleagues here deserve any less money to continue to do their important work. My point is that Brooklyn is in unique need to catch up. When our prosecutors are stretched too thin they have less time to evaluate each case. They have less time to engage victims and witnesses, and they have less time for diversion and restorative justice approaches. I’m asking the Council to address this structural inequity and it is within that context that I ask for your support for these requests this year. First, we’re seeking dedicated funding to combat hate crimes, something I was grateful to discuss with Speaker Menin earlier this month. Brooklyn typically sees among the most hate crimes in the city and our numbers remain up year after year. In fact, we’re up 137 percent in hate crimes in the past five years. When I established a Hate Crimes Bureau in 2018, the first in the city, we didn’t receive any funding for it. We simply

diverted resources from other parts of our office, but because hate crimes have more than doubled since 2018, we need dedicated funding to properly meet this challenge. Of course, you know, much of these hate crimes in Brooklyn, more than 50 percent of those hate crimes are antisemitic hate crimes, and it’s an increasing number of cases each year. We’re also asking for support for our Diversion and Restorative Justice program. These approaches, I think, you know, most of my colleagues here agree, help to produce lower recidivism and higher victim satisfaction, but handling cases with individualized attention requires labor-intensive work. I know many members of the Council at large have expressed interest in Restorative Justice work in particular and I hope you’ll support the investments needed to embed Restorative Justice into the culture of our office. Our budget request this year also includes funding to create a Housing Justice Bureau to protect seniors and others from deed fraud and predatory scams. These crimes can force victims from their homes and rob families of generational wealth. Much of

Brooklyn is ground zero for these cases, especially central Brooklyn. Members of our Brooklyn delegation have raised this issue directly with me because of the impact on vulnerable constituents and we need your support for a comprehensive approach. That would include prevention through education, harm mitigation using appropriate civil tools, and prosecution as appropriate, but this bureau would also do more than simply prosecute people in that thing. It would do some of the work that we really need to see in this city– holding unscrupulous landlords accountable during illegal shut-offs, lock-outs, and other harassing practices that rise to the level of criminality. Many of you have read the stories in the paper where someone will claim there’s a leak, and they’ll come back into their apartment and the landlord had entered their apartment when they weren’t home and removed their kitchen, their bathroom, making the apartment uninhabitable. And I know of you also care about animals as I do, but due to the compression in our budget, we’ve been unable to establish an animal crimes unit. These cases are often heartbreaking and they require

careful coordination with the NYPD and the ASPCA, and extra attention to the evidence which is usually a living animal. We’re asking for funding to create a dedicated unit to ensure these cases receive the attention they deserve. We’re also asking for critical investments in information technology. Our IT staff is less than half the size of other offices, yet, we manage a higher caseload, and we add terabytes of new digital evidence every single day. We cannot handle this growing volume efficiently or safeguard our cyber threats without this investment. It’s critical. And just to put some additional emphasis on it, because we have thousands more cases, our digital needs are even higher, and they’re growing. Just on body cams alone, you know, a terabyte is literally well over 100 iPhones a day. That’s how much volume we’re being asked to store a day, and we have to store it often for 25 years or more. And finally, we’re asking for funding to continue and expand Project Restore. This is the program that the City Council has funded for the last few years, and I want to say thank you. This program gives young people caught in cycles of gang violence a real

offramp. It’s counseling and job skills, life skills, and restorative justice that saves and transforms lives. I think it’s a big part of the reason why Brooklyn has seen a tremendous reduction in shootings and homicides, especially in the area where these programs work. We’ve seen that those areas have seen tremendous declines in shootings. It was launched in Bed-Stuy. Gun violence has gone down there, and we're bringing this model finally to Brownsville. I’d like the City Council to understand that when Columbia University reviewed our program and the great success that it had in transforming lives, it also noted that for every dollar invested into the program, the city saved $6.70 in incarceration and emergency costs. So it’s not just a proven public safety approach that’s in Brooklyn and now coming to the Bronx. It’s also sound fiscal policy. Our work in Brooklyn has also proven that we can lead with safety and fairness, even with the limited resources that we have, but the structural compression of our budget is imperiling that continued progress, so I ask for your support to deal with some of this.

I’ve testified about the structural inequity in our budget before. I am grateful to this City Council for the funding that you did give me last year, especially for project restore and some other programs dealing with domestic violence and youth violence. I grew up in a different Brooklyn than the one that we have today, but I’m looking forward to making sure that we can continue that success. Thank you.

Good afternoon. My name is Melinda Katz. I am the Queens District Attorney. I want to thank you for welcoming us back. I was a Council Member for a lot of years with Michael McMahon. Always nice to be back in the house. I want to congratulate our Chairman, Chairman Feliz, and thank my Council Member from Queens, Phil Wong, for being here and all the other Council Members. I know there’s a lot to do as Council Members, and we appreciate that you have stayed to hear us and our needs and what we hope that we have accomplished as District Attorneys of our counties. So, Queens County is also a very busy county, and what’s interesting is those that are members of Queens know that historically we have been underfunded in a lot

of the issues. It’s not just criminal justice. A lot of its cultural affairs. A lot of it is different subjects that have come up through the years. We had the same fights when I was on the budget negotiations committee 15 years ago, and we continue to have those arguments about Queens. My stats in my office, we have handled 60,000 arrests since 2025. We arraigned 45,000 cases. We resolved 44,000 cases, and we assisted nearly 5,000 victims through our Crime Victims Advocacy. While shooting incidents are down 24 percent overall in the city, Queens County saw a decrease of 25 percent, and while the number of shooting victims citywide decreased 22 percent we saw a decrease in 25 percent. Interestingly enough in my office we also have ADAs that go to almost every crime scene, that is a violent crime scene or a homicide or a vehicular crime scene. In ‘25 we visited 159 homicide crime scenes and 74 vehicular collision cases. So, we do that on a daily basis. It helps when we have ADAs at the scene. It helps the police do the investigation. It helps with our warrants. It

helps to know the case from the very beginning, and we have found that to be priceless in our office. We are asking for an additional $12.5 million, but I’m going to get into that in a second if I can. I would like to go over some of the ways that we have utilized our budget. First of all, in the borough of Queens County we get less per person in almost everything in New York City, right? So, we get on the average about $40 less a resident than any other borough on the average. We get less per arrest. We get less per arraignment, and it has been historical, but I have no doubt that this council will try to help with our inequities, and we would appreciate that. But deposit all that, we have a crime strategies– so we have made getting guns off the street a main priority in Queens County. Our Crime Strategies and Intelligence Bureau continues to lead against the fight of ghost guns. We took 38 percent of the ghost guns off the street last year or the year before and continued it in ‘25. 38 percent of them in the whole City of New York came out of Queens that we got off of the street.

We also worked to make sure that the gangs are investigated and dealt with in a way that helps our young people not be determined to think that gangs are their chosen family. We don’t accept that in Queens county. We don’t accept that hopefully in the City of New York. We have a Violent Criminal Enterprise Bureau that started under my administration. We have taken many investigations and moved them to make sure that we’re not only arresting and getting off the street the gangs, but also working to make sure that any young person that got caught up in it is also getting the help they need to stay out of the criminal justice system, which is why we developed the Gun Diversion Program a few years ago in Queens. The participants in the Gun Diversion Program which is very heavily vetted, by the way, makes sure that they have a year where they’re going to school or they’re working, but also that the rest of their time is taken care of as well with services. We work with the Fortune Society on that. We have found it to be extremely successful in making sure that people graduate from there and don’t end up back in our system.

We’ve also participated in 12 gun buybacks. So we can pro– we can’t prosecute our way out of problems. We also need to do gun buybacks. We’ve gotten 700 guns off the street through a gun buyback, and we are proud of that. That means 700 guns that are not shooting anyone, that are not in the hands of people that are going to utilize them in the community. And so we work closely with the churches and the community on those programs, as well. Retail theft is a huge issue in Queens County. We all know the feeling of standing online waiting to pay your bills. Someone walks in, takes a knapsack and walks out with a bunch of items. We use our Investigations Department to investigate long-term thefts. Last time we arrest– we went and investigated and managed to work and get a Home Depot group of individuals that were going state to state, nine different states, 128 Home Depots, 26– you know, over 2,000 places or items that they went in or incidents that they went in and stole items from a Home Depot from. And we think it’s really important, because that really says a lot to the community. You know, we can

all tell you the gun numbers are down. We can all tell you that shootings are down, but when you’re standing in line at that store and you see someone walking out with items, to you it tends to be 100 percent, because you’re seeing it right in front of you. At the same time, we do have a Bureau of Housing and Worker Protection and we spent a lot of resources on deed theft. Deed theft has become a major issue in Queens County in addition to squatters, and you know, we manage to get people’s homes back. The legislature passed a law about two years ago that allows us to get homes back to third parties who have bought homes that they were not able to buy, and people that sold them had them illegally. So, we work quite often in making sure that we get people’s homes back, you know, homes that they’ve worked for for generations sometimes, and we make sure that we get them back. At the same time, we spent a lot of our resources on the community. We go into the community. We go to the Community Boards. We go to precinct councils so that people feel comfortable referring their cases to us so that there is a knowledge of law enforcement, that we put a face

to law enforcement, that we gain hopefully trust and cooperation from our witnesses and from our victims, and I believe that’s a very important part of what our office does. But that– and we also send people into our schools, and we don’t just send them into junior high schools and high schools, we also send them into elementary schools so that they also put a face on someone that is not an attorney who cares deeply that our youth does not end up in the criminal justice system. And I do have a youth empowerment group that does that every single day, and that’s all they do is work to make sure that our young people don't end up in the criminal justice system, and it has been quite successful. The schools seem to like it. The community groups have them speak at their organizations, and the youth then feel comfortable going to the people we have in the community and asking for help, and their parents or guardians feel comfortable as well approaching us. But all of this is done with less money per individual, per resident, per arrest in the city. So I am requesting money not only for helping out–

because we also have that issue where we pay rent. We are actually 950 people in five locations, some of which we pay rent to, some of which we don’t. And so we spend a lot of money on that as well. But the money that we do need extra is going to fund the Rehabilitation and Restoration Services Bureau, our Crime Victims Advocacy, interpreter staff– we need more interpreter staff. We need people– more people that speak different languages. We are 190 countries and almost 300 languages in the borough of Queens County. I need to be able to service my witnesses and my victims when they come in for help and the defendants when they come in for help to make sure that people understand and that there’s someone that is accessible on those services. For human trafficking, we also have a Bureau of Human Trafficking, which has been unbelievable in researching those individuals that are forced not only into sex trafficking but into labor trafficking as well, forced to work, or forced without pay, pay being held, passports being held. So we want to expand those services as well. The details of our funding application is in my testimony

that we have handed to you. I can only say that we try to do justice at every level with any amount of money we have. It would certainly be a better thing for our office if we were able to spend the money not only on prosecution, but also on making sure we keep people out of the criminal justice system. I do believe that we are owed– we owe our constituents that as a balance. I thank the Council for our funding for last year, for– we got money for a crime lab, which will be unbelievably helpful in making sure that we’re able to download phones and computers, and we can do it right on site, and so thank you for being so responsive to that request. And I look forward to working with you this year as well. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair and members of the committee. I’m Alvin Bragg, the District Attorney for New York County. Unlike DA Katz and McMahon, I was not a member, but I was staffer. So I also want to thank not just the members, but the incredible staff here at the Council. I’ll start with just data about Manhattan as my colleagues have, and it’s encouraging. There’s more

work to do. But in 2025, total index crime in Manhattan was down four percent from 2024, and down 13 percent from 2022 which outpaces the citywide decreases. The data on violent crime is particularly encouraging. Homicides are down almost 50 percent compared to four years ago. Last year, the 53 homicides reported in Manhattan were 22 fewer than in 2024 and on par with pre-pandemic levels. We’re encouraged thus far to see that trend continuing this year with three homicides in the borough as of March 15th compared to nine. The data on shootings is very encouraging, almost a 70 percent decrease in shootings in Manhattan since 2021, the last four years. Shooting incidents were down 38 percent in 2025 compared to 2024, and notably, if you compare it to the pre-pandemic levels, we’re down 25 percent in shootings compared to the pre-pandemic levels of 2019. District Attorney Gonzalez mentioned East New York. He and I often compare notes. I grew up in Central Harlem which historically is the part of the borough with the most violence. I still live there. We see the

benefits of this progress, but we have a lot more work to do. I wanted to highlight three areas of our work and then specifically highlight some of the asks in the written testimony. The first is hate crimes, and it comes with a very big thank you which is a recurring theme from Manhattan to this Council. A few years ago we requested and were given $1.7 million by the Council to expand our Hate Crimes Unit. We went from two to 15 specially-trained prosecutors. We hired new investigators and new analysts. We expanded our community outreach. The funding that you provided us has helped our Survivor Services Bureau, hire and retain victim service advocates with cultural competency to assist the Jewish, AAPI, Muslim, and LGBTQ communities. We’re profoundly grateful for that money and the funding to the work. We’re encouraged that Manhattan reported hate crimes were down 30 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. We know it’s an under-reported crime. We will continue to do the outreach and continue to support, but I wanted to thank the Council and report back on what we’ve been doing with the funding you provided.

Second, retail theft– again, the numbers are heading in the right direction in Manhattan, but there’s more work to do. Retail theft complaints were down 11 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. This is in part due to the work of our Manhattan Small Business Alliance. We’ve brought together small business owners, BIDs, law enforcement, and service providers to target our efforts. We’ve zeroed in on those who are doing this conduct over and over with a focused deterrent strategy, and then 2025, we prosecuted 6,700 misdemeanor retail cases and another 1,800 felony retail cases. We’re getting people into meaningful treatment for drug and mental health issues through our Pathways to Public Safety Division when appropriate, and where appropriate we’re seeking incarceration. In addition to sort of this day-in/day-out work, we’re also following the money. DA Katz talked about work she’s doing in Queens. Similarly in Manhattan, we’re actually scheduled to go to trial shortly this year on a case against a brother and sister tandem that were– we allege operating a fencing operation

with approximately $1 million in stolen goods. So, that complements our approach to retail theft. Third, worker and tenant protection, and again this comes with a very, very big thank you. Funding from the Council helped us start our Worker Protection Unit and helps us continue to stand up for hardworking New Yorkers and hold accountable companies that are lining their pockets at the expense of employees. So, just to report back, in 2025 indictments resulted in nearly $600,000 being returned to 22 workers from unscrupulous employers. We were also able to return over $1.4 million to the New York State Insurance Fund through eight cases prosecuting companies that defrauded the fund by failing to pay proper workers compensation insurance premiums. We all know about the affordable housing crisis in the city and in Manhattan, and our Tenant Protection Unit has been focusing on criminal misconduct by landlords. The cases we’ve brought include charges for abusing governmental affordable housing programs like 421A, tenant harassment, deed fraud, and rental scams. Just by way of one example, we indicted and are prosecuting Daniel Phillam [sp?]

and his companies for multiple counts of harassment of rent regulated tenant in the first degree, and we’ll continue this important work with your support. Now, I just- I want to sort of just raise up from the written testimony three specific asks. One relates to our domestic violence work and our Special Victims Division. As I think we all know, domestic violence is among the most common– among one of the most common crimes in New York City in the nation. Yet, it is still under-reported. When I took office, I created the Special Victims Division which houses our Intimate Partner and Special Violence Bureau. And again, I want to thank the Council for providing funding for our Survivor Services Bureau. That work is so essential to all that we do, but in particular our domestic violence and intimate partner violence work. Just to put some numbers on this– in New York City, domestic violence comprises about 40 percent of all felony crimes. As of March 12th of this year in Manhattan we have more than 1,600 intimate partner violence cases pending, including about 500 felony intimate partner violence cases.

And again, we know there’s under-reporting in this area. We know that there’s a lot more to do in terms of outreach. One strategy that we’ve piloted and we’d like additional funding to expand is our Early Engagement Team. We’ve identified– we are identifying lower level intimate partner violence offenses that could signal a high risk of escalation to more serious violence, and then responding to these high-risk situations with urgency and appropriate resources including a team of prosecutors, analysts, investigators, and victim advocates working closely with the NYPD to review domestic incident reports before there’s even an arrest. That team works to connect with survivors and provide support and resources, and at the same time we are investigating alongside the NYPD. We’ve piloted it. We’d like to expand it. We need additional resources for our Special Victims Division to support that work. So that’s one additional ask. Second relates to mental health and the work of our Pathways Division which has been focused on this, and I think we all know the brokenness of our mental health system. If you go to probably any of our

criminal courts, but I’ll speak for Manhattan, you’ll see that on full display. I’m proud to continue though in the success of our Pathways to Public Safety Division which again this Council has helped support. Those prosecutors are proactively screening all of our street crime cases, felony cases in 48 hours of arraignment and reviewing thousands of misdemeanor cases each year. Cases considered are reviewed individually and holistically in conjunction with independent clinical records. With the creation of the division, my office has more than doubled felony problem-solving court referrals. Close to a quarter of our indicted felony defendants in Manhattan awaiting a felony disposition on track to take a plea at one of the four felony problem-solving courts. And our record of success is clear based on encouraging data to date, shows lower recidivism rates than when compared with other approaches and it’s making Manhattan safer. And the idea behind the Hope Program is– and piggybacking on what DA Clark said, is that someone would be met at the precinct by a peer navigator at the moment of arrest even before booking and given an offer of a diversion program that would be tailored just for them if they agreed to meaningfully engage for 30 days– the case would be dismissed, and that program has expanded.
